About MyDogCanFly — who's behind the data
Who publishes MyDogCanFly, how the airline, country and breed data is sourced and verified, and our editorial standards.

MyDogCanFly is a data-driven, bilingual platform that helps people fly safely and legally with their dog. We do not sell tickets or give veterinary opinions — we compile, structure and verify the official rules so you can decide with confidence.
How we source and verify data

Every airline policy, country entry rule and breed travel profile is built from primary, official sources — airline pet-travel pages, national veterinary authorities, USDA APHIS export pages, the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and EU regulations. Two rules govern the whole site: nothing is fabricated, and where an official source does not publish a fact we mark it "Unknown" rather than guessing. Each record carries its source, a verification date and a confidence level.

Our tools (flight finder, heat-risk, crate size, travel timeline, airport relief) derive their verdicts from this data with a transparent rules engine — the reasoning is always shown, never a black box.

MyDogCanFly is founded and edited by Phil Albert-Benoist, who is also its director of publication. His background bridges digital engineering (EFREI Paris) and visual culture (ENSP Arles): the technical foundations of a rigorous, structured, standards-compliant web platform, paired with a demanding editorial eye. Day-to-day this means platform architecture, Schema.org structured data, SEO and GEO (optimisation for search and for generative engines), bilingual editorial governance and privacy compliance.
The editorial line, sourcing standards, verification methodology and accuracy of published information are under his direct supervision.

Airline, country and breed rankings are computed from the data — they are never sold or influenced by payment. Where the site earns from affiliate links (for example travel-crate or partner recommendations), those links are clearly disclosed and do not change the underlying verdicts.

Destination {0}: the certificate to obtain is the one that country requires — see step 2. On the departure side, {1} issues or endorses it: allow for the lead time and book before your flight.

Two possible routes here, and a single document separates them: an EU pet passport already in order before the dog left the EU removes the need for an EU animal health certificate. As long as that is not settled, both are shown.

Your dog comes back on its EU pet passport alone, with no EU animal health certificate, provided that passport — completed by an authorised veterinarian — establishes that BEFORE it left the EU the dog already met the rabies vaccination conditions and, where applicable, the rabies antibody titration test. It still needs its ISO microchip and a rabies vaccination valid on the day of travel; a booster given abroad can be entered in Section V of the passport by an authorised veterinarian. If any of these elements cannot be established from the passport, the EU animal health certificate applies instead. Two limits: this covers a stay abroad, not a change of residence — once you habitually reside outside the EU the passport can no longer be used, whatever your nationality or property in the EU; and a passport issued to an owner resident in Great Britain has not been valid for travel to the EU since 31 December 2020.

With that passport there is no EU animal health certificate to have issued and endorsed here before the flight to the EU — the dog travels on its passport. Check only that the rabies vaccination is still valid on the day of the flight: a booster given abroad can be entered in Section V of the passport by an authorised veterinarian.

Special cases & reserves — check if they apply to you
Brachycephalic breed (bulldog, pug…): hold often refused, especially in summer.
Puppy under 12 weeks: the rabies vaccine cannot be given before that age, and nearly every country requires it.
Recent stay (6 months) in a high-rabies-risk country: stricter entry (permit/titer).
Layover in a third country: the applicable rule can change — check the whole itinerary, not just the two ends.
Several animals or a commercial purpose: switches to the commercial regime, other rules.
Puppy under 12 weeks or not yet vaccinated: travel to the EU is not possible.
Layover through a non-listed third country: a rabies titer may then become mandatory to enter the EU.
More than 5 animals or commercial purpose: the EU switches to the commercial regime, other rules.
